periods.analysis: We are starting this eight-quarter view at 2,100 people counted as unsheltered, which is 100 over the <=2,000 target and correctly in yellow. The count was completed on schedule with Outreach, Police Community Response, Parks, and the Harborview Housing Authority using the shared GIS route book, including the Airport Way, South Seaport, and Canal Greenway zones. Data quality is solid for Council reporting: duplicate checks were completed against HMIS IDs and the volunteer canvass logs, with the main watch-item being repeat observations along the waterfront trail. The result is not where we want it, but it gives us a clean baseline for measuring whether shelter diversion, motel exits, and housing navigation are actually bending the curve.
periods.recommendations: Keep the monthly reconciliation meeting on the first Tuesday so Housing, Fire CARE, Parks, and the airport outreach vendor close data issues before the quarterly packet deadline. Add two evening outreach sweeps on the Route 14 bus corridor and Canal Greenway before the next count, because those locations drove most of the uncertainty. For Council, frame this as a yellow early-warning item with a clear target: move at least 100 people into documented shelter, reunification, or housing placements before 2024-Q4.

periods.analysis: The count rose from 2,100 to 2,180, an increase of 80 quarter over quarter, keeping us in yellow but moving in the wrong direction. The seasonal pattern is visible: colder nights shifted people toward the airport perimeter, ferry terminal overhangs, and the South Seaport industrial frontage, where crews logged more repeat contacts. I want us to be precise here: the increase is real, not just better counting, because HMIS match rates stayed stable and the same zone teams covered the same routes. The watch-item for Council is that winter shelter demand is outpacing exits from the Navigation Center, even though the Harbor Inn motel block kept several families from appearing in the unsheltered total.
periods.recommendations: Extend the Harbor Inn and Bayview Lodge motel blocks through the end of winter and require weekly exit plans for every room, not just occupancy counts. Assign the Community Response Team a standing Thursday evening route at the airport light-rail station, ferry terminal, and Seaport Gate 3) Bring a short variance memo to the next Council committee showing the 80-person movement and the specific winter operations being used to keep yellow from becoming red.

periods.analysis: The count increased again, from 2,180 to 2,240, a quarter-over-quarter increase of 60, so we remain yellow and still above the <=2,000 target. The smaller increase compared with last quarter is useful, but I would not call it a trend yet; Q1 weather, post-holiday service gaps, and lease-up timing all distort the count. Operations did improve: the CARE van completed 312 contacts on the Airport Way and Midtown Library loops, and the housing navigators closed several duplicate records before the scorecard deadline. The watch-item is the growing gap between people accepting shelter referrals and people actually arriving, especially on weekend referrals after 5 p.m.
periods.recommendations: Pilot a 72-hour referral hold with transport confirmation for the 40 highest-frequency outreach contacts identified in HMIS. Have the Navigation Center and the airport outreach vendor send Friday noon bed-availability files to Jamie’s scorecard team so we are not cleaning up avoidable data gaps after quarter close. Continue the same route methodology next quarter so Council can compare 2025-Q2 to 2025-Q1 without a methodology footnote.

periods.analysis: The count moved from 2,240 to 2,300, another increase of 60, which places Harborview exactly at the top edge of yellow. This is the last safe quarter before the threshold turns red, and I want that stated plainly in the Council narrative. The increase was concentrated in the Canal Greenway, East Basin underpasses, and the Route 22 transfer area, while the downtown core was comparatively stable after the Clean Corridors team paired storage outreach with trash service. The data file was submitted on time, and department coordination was good, but the operating picture says our placement velocity is still not matching inflow.
periods.recommendations: Treat 2,300 as the trigger point for a 90-day Unsheltered Stabilization Sprint led by Housing with weekly attendance from Parks, Police Community Response, Public Works, and the airport authority. Prioritize 125 document-ready individuals for rapid lease-up at Harbor Landing, Mariner Court, and scattered-site vouchers before the next count. Ask Council to authorize a limited summer storage-and-hygiene expansion at East Basin and Route 22, tied to outreach participation and verified placement outcomes.

periods.analysis: The count crossed into red, rising from 2,300 to 2,360, a quarter-over-quarter increase of 60 and now above the >2,300 red threshold. That is a serious movement, but it is also actively managed: the Stabilization Sprint stood up weekly case conferences, and the first Housing Pipeline Renewal list identified lease-up bottlenecks by project, unit type, and inspection date. The clearest pressure points were East Basin, the Canal Greenway, and the airport employee lot edges, where outreach teams reported more people living in vehicles and makeshift structures. For Council, the message should be direct: we protected data integrity and coordination, but the system needs faster exits, not just more contacts.
periods.recommendations: Move Housing Pipeline Renewal from tracking to action by assigning named owners to every stalled unit at Harbor Landing Phase II, Seaview Supportive Housing, and the North Pier master-lease block. Add a twice-weekly inspection fast lane with Building and Fire for units reserved for unsheltered placements. Maintain the weekly red-status stand-up until the count is back at or below 2,300, and publish a short placement dashboard with inflow, exits, and failed referrals.

periods.analysis: The count increased from 2,360 to 2,410, a quarter-over-quarter increase of 50, so we remain red even though the rate of increase eased. The moderation matters, and departments deserve credit for consistent execution, but 2,410 is still 410 above target and too high for a city with Harborview’s capacity and AA-rated financial footing. Winter operations opened the Civic Annex overflow beds and extended the Bayview Lodge contract, while Housing Pipeline Renewal cleared several inspection holds at Mariner Court. The main watch-item is churn: people are being contacted and referred, but too many placements are delayed by documents, pet accommodations, or unit-readiness issues.
periods.recommendations: Stand up a document clinic every Wednesday at the Civic Annex with the county recorder, DMV liaison, and benefits navigator focused on the current unsheltered cohort. Reserve a small pet-friendly room block and track it separately, because refusals tied to pets are showing up repeatedly in the case notes. Keep the red-status cadence, but add a Council-facing milestone: 75 verified housing exits from the 2025-Q4 cohort before the 2026-Q1 count.

periods.analysis: The count rose from 2,410 to 2,450, a quarter-over-quarter increase of 40, which is still red but shows a second quarter of slower growth. I am encouraged by the direction of the rate, not the level: 2,450 remains 450 above the <=2,000 target. The best operational news is that Housing Pipeline Renewal reduced the oldest unit-readiness holds, and the CARE team’s airport-to-shelter transport protocol cut missed referrals on the late shift. The remaining pressure is highly concentrated in vehicle encampments near Port Access Road and the East Basin viaduct, where flood-prone conditions also create public safety risk during king tide events.
periods.recommendations: Create a vehicle-resolution cohort for Port Access Road and East Basin with 50 named households, paired with safe-parking, repair assistance, and direct housing navigation. Keep the airport late-shift transport protocol in place and extend it to the ferry terminal during spring break travel weeks. Ask Public Works and Housing to jointly flag tidal-flooding encampment locations in the next operational map so relocations are planned, humane, and not improvised during storms.

periods.analysis: The count increased from 2,450 to 2,487, a quarter-over-quarter increase of 37, which keeps the measure in red despite the smallest increase in this eight-quarter arc. That slowing is meaningful, and it suggests the case-conference model, motel exits, and Housing Pipeline Renewal work are starting to reduce acceleration. Still, 2,487 is 487 above the <=2,000 target, so Council should hear both truths: the curve is flattening, and the absolute level remains unacceptable. The Q2 file was closed on time with clean zone reconciliation, and the highest-growth pockets were again vehicle encampments and underpass locations rather than the downtown core.
periods.recommendations: Convert the 90-day red-status stand-up into a six-month Unsheltered Reduction Plan with monthly Council reporting on placements, inflow, unit readiness, and repeat contacts. Expand Housing Pipeline Renewal to include landlord recruitment for 100 additional shallow-subsidy units near Route 14, Route 22, and the airport employment corridor. Sustain the data discipline that got us a clean Q2 file, but require every red pocket to have a named field lead, next action date, and target exit pathway before the next quarterly close.

periods.analysis: The unsheltered component increased from 1,268 to 1,276, above its lower-is-better target of 1,150. Emergency shelter and transitional housing are reported separately; none of these entries establishes a reduction in unsheltered need.
periods.recommendations: Continue zone reconciliation and review placements, inflow and repeat contacts before describing a change in the broader point-in-time count.
